items.title: Robert Macfarlane says trust in Cop to deliver change on climate is ‘misplaced’
items.summary_raw:
Nature writer reveals in his first Reith lecture that he finds ‘much more hope’ in emerging alliances

We are “misplacing our trust” in the Cop climate summits and their “capacity to deliver consequential change”, according to Robert Macfarlane in this year’s Reith lectures.

In comments recorded before this week’s failure of the 31st UN climate summit to deliver an agreement on action to combat global heating, the bestselling author said he saw “much more hope” in emerging alliances such as the Santa Marta process, which is a smaller group of countries committed to phasing out fossil fuels as soon as possible.

items.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
items.summary_raw:
Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action

In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend.

Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. items.title: The good news out of Cop31? That most of the world’s governments said no to an agreement stripped of meaning | Bill Hare
items.summary_raw:
Co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia, which is exporting climate pain

The failure of Cop31 in Antalya was a line in the sand moment, a victory for multiculturalism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no. The text they rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.

The good news is that most of the world’s governments rejected an agreement stripped of meaning. And the power of one particular fossil fuel producer, Saudi Arabia, needs particular scrutiny. What we also know is that co-chairing global climate talks is clearly not something to be repeated, certainly not by Australia. It didn’t work.

items.summary_raw:
Two supertankers hit mines near Hormuz, Iranian navy says

Iran's navy said on Sunday that two supertankers hit naval mines and caught fire after entering a "restricted area" east of the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian media reported.

According to the Fars news agency, the navy said the tankers had switched off their detection and navigation systems and struck the mines north of Ghanam Island.

Both vessels reportedly stopped moving.

Supertankers usually carry two million barrels of oil or more, about twice as much as a standard tanker.

The navy also warned that relying on "smugglers such as CENTCOM", referring to US Central Command, would result in "nothing but heavy losses".

items.summary_raw:
The Cop31 climate talks fell into disarray as the EU, UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate. Ireland's climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, said the EU could not support the proposed deal, in part because it made no mention of fossil fuels. The president of the negotiations, Australia's Chris Bowen, called the failure 'very disappointing', saying that a lot of good work had been done but 'many parties who were people of good faith had very strong red lines on a couple of key issues, and despite many, many attempts … those red lines on behalf of different parties were just not able to be met'.

Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject climate deal over fossil fuels

The United Nations climate summit in Turkey became the longest-ever UN climate conference on Sunday as negotiations over a final agreement descended into deadlock, with the European Union and several other countries formally rejecting the proposed text.

The talks in Antalya, known as Cop31, continued more than 44 hours beyond their scheduled Friday conclusion, surpassing the previous record set by Cop25 in Madrid in 2019.

The latest draft, presented by the Turkish and Australian presidencies in an attempt to bridge divisions between countries, failed to secure consensus over its omission of explicit references to fossil fuels and disagreements over climate finance.

Good Morning Middle East Eye readers,

If you are just joining us, here are key developments from across the region and beyond:

*Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says its forces attacked two US bases in Bahrain; Manama says strikes hit civilian industrial facility.

*The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by Yemen's Houthis towards Saudi Arabia's western region.

*Two Palestinians injured in an Israeli strike on Gaza succumb as territory's health ministry says death toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” rises to 1,661.

items.title: Turkey says Israel blocking thousands of container homes from entering Gaza
items.summary_raw:
Turkey says Israel blocking thousands of container homes from entering Gaza

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said Israel is blocking thousands of container homes destined for Gaza, adding that Israeli authorities argue Hamas could use the metal structures  for manufacturing weapons.

Fidan told Turkish broadcaster TGRT Haber on Saturday that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had ordered the temporary housing units, which Turkey used during the earthquake, to be sent to the Palestinian enclave.

He said Israeli restrictions were leaving displaced Palestinians dependent on fabric tents, exposing them to flooding, storms and cold weather.

“When floods, storms or cold weather come, they cause a disaster at least as devastating as hunger, if not more so,” he said.

They are seeking to provoke the Syrian army, and there is a scenario in which the Israeli army could use this as a pretext to launch a military operation against Syria.

Some are fleeing, some are coming to work.  Many came who do not like us, who do not like homosexuals, who do not agree with equality for women, who believe that their own religion, Islam, should stand above democracy.  They use violence as a legitimate tool in raising their children, against women, and against others in the streets.  And that dominance culture is dangerous. I say that as a Social Democrat, I say it as a woman, I say it as a Dane.   But I also say it as prime minister of a country where that dominance culture is incompatible with the way we have built our society.

items.summary_raw:
Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035

  • Cop31 live – latest updates

China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

The Senate approved bipartisan legislation on Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure datacenters pay for the energy they use. Anger over datacenters and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

Its crew had spent the past 12 days at sea, recording mammal sightings, monitoring vessels to ensure they didn’t enter construction zones, and keeping watch over workers at Revolution Wind, a 65-turbine offshore wind project just south of Rhode Island.

items.title: How the war in Iran turned the Gulf into a climate catastrophe – video explainer
items.summary_raw:
The war between the US, Israel and Iran has turned the strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes, into a battlefield, but also the centre of a deepening environmental disaster. Tankers struck by missiles or sea mines are leaking oil into the Gulf, leaving vast slicks visible from space, staining coastlines and threatening lasting damage to marine ecosystems. Many of these areas remain inaccessible because of the naval blockade, making it virtually impossible to document the devastation on the ground. The Guardian has examined dozens of satellite images and spoken to environmental experts in an effort to assess the scale of the damage

items.title: ‘The Pacific is not for sale’: outcry after US holds first deep sea mining lease sale near American Samoa

Multi-million dollar sale comes despite a federal judge in Hawaii voiding the environmental clearance it had been given to proceed

The US has carried out its first ever deep-sea mining lease sales off the coast of American Samoa, despite an adverse court ruling earlier this week and mounting local opposition.

The sales took place on Thursday in a live-streamed auction of 12.7m hectares (31.5m acres) of seabed off the US territory’s coast marked for mineral exploration. Two areas of the Pacific archipelago were sold for $3m each to Wetstone US Ventures, the only bidder, according to a spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration (MMA).

items.title: Cop31 live: Fossil fuels dumped from latest draft deal at climate summit
items.summary_raw:
The latest draft text has been published, as negotiations continue at the UN summit in Turkey

Ethiopia can show that taking strong action to solve the climate crisis can go along with economic growth in the developing world, the president-designate of next year’s Cop has said.

“Climate action and development and progress are not mutually exclusive,” Gedion Timothewos told the Guardian in an interview at Cop31. “Good economic policy, that has a positive impact on people’s pockets, and on GDP and your economy, can also be good climate action. That is something we believe the Ethiopian experience can showcase.”

Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned.

Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems.

items.title: Cop31 live: rich world offering ‘crumbs’ to help poor countries adapt to climate breakdown, campaigners say

Wealthy polluters promised to put $50m into an adaptation fund this week, less than half of what countries promised at last year’s climate summit

California Governor Gavin Newsom was a big presence in Antalya last week, serving as the head of a US delegation that attended unofficially due to President Donald Trump’s withdrawal from the international summit.

Widely seen as a top presidential contender for 2028, Newsom’s strong rhetoric in support of a fossil fuel phase out and other top climate priorities inspired hope that there’s a future for the US – the world’s second biggest emitter – in negotiations. That of course, depends on who ends up as the next resident of the White House, but Newsom made big promises regardless, as the head of California – the world’s fourth largest economy.

items.title: UK backs idea of new levies on polluting sectors to pay for climate action costs
items.summary_raw:
Britain joins other signatories to statement urging introduction of targeted taxes on heavy emitters

The UK has signed a statement that backs levies on polluting sectors to pay for the impacts of the climate crisis, in a strong political signal that could pave the way for frequent flyer and crypto taxes.

Signing the statement at the UN climate summit means the UK joins a group of governments urging Cop31 to look at “the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors”. The other signatories so far are Kenya, South Sudan, Spain, Timor Leste, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

items.summary_raw:
Thorny divisions emerge as wide-ranging draft deal seeks to ‘draw out parties’ on areas of disagreement

Speaking at a press conference just now, the EU’s climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, lamented the language on climate finance, trade and carbon capture (CCS) in the draft decision. He argued that the focus of this Cop was supposed to be on implementation. “It had the characteristics of a shopping list,” he said of yesterday’s text.

“That, in our view, is fundamentally at odds with the logic of implementation,” he added. “Delivering what we have already agreed on, that should be the focus. And that is why we do think that – particularly in the domain of finance, particularly in the domain of trade, also in the domain of CCS, and suggesting that might be the solution to everything – I think the cover decision does not go in the right direction and needs significant change.”

  • Miatta Fahnbulleh is the UK secretary of state for energy security and net zero

In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.

That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. items.title: What do you want to know about the Cop31 climate talks? Ask Fiona Harvey and Ajit Niranjan
items.summary_raw:
The Guardian’s environment editor Fiona Harvey and Europe environment correspondent Ajit Niranjan will answer your questions on Cop31, the draft deal on fossil fuels, the fight over climate finance and what overshooting 1.5C means for the world.

Ask a question: log in or sign up here

The Cop31 climate summit in Antalya is in its final days, and negotiators are fighting over a first draft of the deal.

It calls for “accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”, and for tripling adaptation finance for poorer countries. But with the world heading past the 1.5C limit and countries deeply divided over finance, adaptation and the “just transition”, can Cop31 deliver anything that matters?

Το κείμενο έχει ήδη διαβιβαστεί στην ηγεσία της Ευρωπαϊκής Επιτροπής, του Ευρωπαϊκού Συμβουλίου, του Ευρωπαϊκού Κοινοβουλίου, της Ιρλανδικής Προεδρίας της ΕΕ και της Ευρωπαϊκής Τράπεζας Επενδύσεων.
